Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Mateo, a 22-year-old HVAC technician, vividly recalled the day his life irrevocably shifted. It had been just a few months ago, a bright but brisk morning on a commercial rooftop. He was operating the hoist, meticulously maneuvering a heavy condensing unit into its designated spot. For a brief, unnerving moment, an unusual silence fell across the rooftop, the kind that makes the hairs on the back of your neck stand up. It was in that profound quiet, just before the unit was fully secured, that a sharp, metallic crack echoed through the air. The hoist mechanism failed, and the massive unit swung violently, striking his coworker, Luis, who was guiding it from below. Mateo remembered the metallic tang in the air, mixed with the acrid smell of ozone and a faint whiff of refrigerant as he rushed forward, his own body feeling strangely disconnected from the chaos.

In the immediate aftermath, the memory of the accident felt strangely distant, almost as if he had watched it unfold from a remove, like a scene from a movie where someone else was operating the controls. This detachment persisted; even now, when the images forced their way into his mind when he least expected them, the memory felt alien, as if it belonged to someone else rather than to him. Despite this, he found himself relentlessly overanalysing, going over and over the details of the event, scrutinizing every micro-second leading up to the hoist’s failure, desperate to make sense of it, yet finding no peace. He had come to believe he would never forgive himself for not reacting faster, for not doing more to stop what happened, a profound and heavy inaction guilt settling over him.

The incident shattered his self-perception. His hands, once a source of pride for their strength and precision in his trade, now felt like instruments of betrayal. He could no longer trust his own body, seeing it as unreliable, prone to catastrophic failure at critical moments. Looking in the mirror, the person staring back felt unrecognisable to him; the confident, capable HVAC technician he once was had been replaced by someone haunted and hesitant.

Now, Mateo felt safe only in a very limited number of places—his small apartment, his parents’ house, and the well-worn routes between them. The world outside these zones felt fraught with hidden dangers. Any unusual silence, particularly when he was on a job site or in an unfamiliar building, would trigger an immediate, visceral fear that something dangerous was about to happen, sending his heart racing and his palms sweating. He experienced strong physical reactions, a sudden jolt of adrenaline and muscle tension, whenever something—even a mundane clang of metal from a nearby construction site or the distant hum of a crane—reminded him of the stressful experience.

To cope, Mateo began to avoid anything that could be stressful. He started turning down more complex installations at work, especially those involving heavy lifting or working at heights, often citing vague excuses. This meant less challenging, lower-paying assignments, and a growing distance from his colleagues who found his sudden reluctance to take on responsibility confusing. He went out of his way to avoid dates or anniversaries connected to the event, scheduling shifts on those days, or simply staying home, disconnecting from his phone and social life. This self-imposed isolation, while seemingly protecting him from further distress, left him feeling increasingly alone.

The cumulative weight of these changes eventually became unbearable. He found himself spending most evenings staring blankly at the TV, his mind either racing with replays of the accident or consumed by a pervasive sense of dread. The thought of a specific date approaching, marking the six-month anniversary of Luis’s accident, filled him with a terror he could no longer manage alone. He realised he couldn’t continue living this way, trapped by a past that felt both alien and intensely personal, a past that had stolen the person he once was. It was this desperate hope for some measure of relief, for a way to reconcile with the unrecognisable self he had become, that finally led him to seek help.
